title: Introduction to database systems
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs expect candidates to separate database from DBMS, explain why a DBMS beats bare files, and name the main data models before diving into SQL or schema design.
company_notes: Widely used systems named in the notes: Oracle (9i, 11g, 12c), Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, and IBM DB2.

phases.goal: Establish what a database, a DBMS, and a database system are, and what kinds of data they manage.

must_hit.point: A database system has two cooperating parts: the database (the data) and the DBMS (the software that operates on that data).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explicitly separates data from the software layer and says together they form a database system.

must_hit.point: A database is an organised collection of related data about some domain, not a heap of arbitrary files.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions organised/related data and gives a domain example such as railway reservation or university records.

must_hit.point: A DBMS stores, retrieves, updates and protects data and mediates access to it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists storage/retrieval/update/protection and access mediation as DBMS responsibilities.

must_hit.point: Managed data ranges from highly structured tabular records through unstructured data to raw web pages; an RDBMS specialises in structured tabular data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes structured vs unstructured/web-page data and ties RDBMS to tables.

probes: What is the difference between a database and a DBMS?
What kinds of data can a database system manage, and what is an RDBMS specialised for?

hints.1: Think of the data collection versus the software that operates on it.
hints.2: Define database, define DBMS, then say what they form together; mention structured versus unstructured data.
hints.3: A database is organised related data; a DBMS stores, manipulates and controls access; together they are a database system; RDBMS targets structured tabular data.

phases.goal: Explain how a DBMS improves on a file system along structure, concurrency, security and redundancy.

must_hit.point: A DBMS stores data with explicit structure—named attributes (columns) of defined types—whereas a file system imposes no such structure on the bytes it holds.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts named typed attributes/columns with unstructured file bytes.

must_hit.point: A DBMS coordinates four kinds of overlapping access between two transactions: read–read (RR), read–write (RW), write–read (WR) and write–write (WW).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all four overlap kinds (RR, RW, WR, WW) as what concurrency control must handle.

must_hit.point: A DBMS enforces fine-grained role-based access control so different roles (for example student, faculty, dean) see and may touch only appropriate data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes RBAC and that the same underlying data is exposed differently by role.

must_hit.point: A DBMS reduces redundancy from scattered duplicate facts and the inconsistencies that duplication breeds.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links file-side duplication to inconsistency and DBMS to reduced redundancy.

probes: How does a DBMS control concurrent access that a file system does not?
How does role-based access control change what different users see?

hints.1: Compare bare files to a DBMS on structure, many users, and who may see what.
hints.2: Cover attributes/types, the four conflict kinds RR/RW/WR/WW, and roles like student/faculty/dean.
hints.3: DBMS adds typed attributes, concurrency over RR/RW/WR/WW, RBAC by role, and less duplicated inconsistent data.

phases.goal: Contrast the file-system approach with a DBMS on the axes the notes treat as advantages.

must_hit.point: Flat files are comfortable for small amounts of data (a few kilobytes) but degrade as data grows; a DBMS is built to organise and query very large volumes (gigabytes and far beyond).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the kilobytes-versus-gigabytes scale contrast between files and DBMS.

must_hit.point: The advantages of a DBMS over a file system are scale, enforced structure, concurrency control, security through role-based access, and reduced redundancy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those five advantage axes in one coherent answer.

probes: Why prefer a DBMS over storing application data in ordinary files?
On which axes does a DBMS beat a file system?

hints.1: List what goes wrong when many users and large data live in plain files.
hints.2: Walk scale, structure, concurrency, security, and redundancy one by one.
hints.3: Files suit small kilobyte data with no structure/concurrency/RBAC; DBMS wins on gigabyte-scale, attributes, RR/RW/WR/WW control, role-based security, and less redundancy.

phases.goal: Place the relational model among the named data-model families and know when RDBMS thinking applies.

must_hit.point: A data model is the abstract framework that determines how data is structured and related.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines data model as the structuring/relating framework, not a vendor product.

must_hit.point: The course names five families: network (owner–member graph), hierarchical (parent–child tree), relational (tables of rows and columns—the dominant model), entity–relationship (high-level design of entities and relationships), and object-oriented (data as objects).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the five models with a one-line characterisation of each, stressing relational as dominant.

must_hit.point: Structured domain examples such as a railway booking system (for example IRCTC) or university student records are the natural fit for an RDBMS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties tabular structured domains to RDBMS rather than treating all data the same.

probes: What data models does the course name, and which one underlies these notes?
When would you reach for an RDBMS rather than treating data as unstructured files or web pages?

hints.1: Recall the historical model families and which one uses tables.
hints.2: List network, hierarchical, relational, ER, and object-oriented with a short structural cue for each.
hints.3: Five models: network graph, hierarchical tree, relational tables (dominant), ER design model, OO objects; RDBMS fits structured tabular domains like bookings or student records.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Files are fine for small kilobyte-scale unstructured blobs but lack typed attributes, concurrency control over RR/RW/WR/WW, role-based access (student/faculty/dean), and anti-redundancy discipline; a DBMS is built for gigabyte-scale organised related data with those controls.

tradeoffs.topic: Structured RDBMS data vs unstructured or web-page data
tradeoffs.strong_answer: An RDBMS specialises in structured tabular data with named attributes; database systems may also hold unstructured content and raw web pages, but those are outside the relational specialisation.

gotchas.correction: The database is the organised related data; the DBMS is the software that stores, manipulates and controls access; together they are the database system.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a file system provides concurrency and fine-grained security comparable to a DBMS.
gotchas.correction: File systems do not coordinate RR/RW/WR/WW overlaps or express role-based access the way a DBMS does.

gotchas.trap: Treating the ER model as another physical storage model alongside relational tables.
gotchas.correction: ER is a high-level design model of entities and relationships; the relational model is the dominant storage/query model of tables of rows and columns.

gotchas.trap: Saying a DBMS only stores structured rows and columns.
gotchas.correction: Managed data ranges from structured records through unstructured data to raw web pages; RDBMS is the variety specialised for structured tabular data.
